name: Shivaji
info: Shivaji I (c. 1630-1680), of the Bhonsle family, turned his father's jagir near Pune into the Maratha Kingdom, fought the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire with hill forts and guerrilla tactics, and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674.

facts.born: c. 19 February 1630 (scholars disagree on the date) at the hill-fort of Shivneri near Junnar; son of the Maratha general Shahaji Bhonsle and Jijabai
facts.died: around 3-5 April 1680 at Raigad Fort, after an illness with fever and dysentery; the cause is disputed
facts.role: Holder of the Pune jagir from 1647; Mughal vassal under the Treaty of Purandar, 1665; Raja by Mughal grant, 1666-1668; Chhatrapati of the Maratha Kingdom, 1674-1680
facts.known: founding the Maratha Kingdom; the killing of Afzal Khan at Pratapgad; the sacks of Surat; escape from Agra; coronation at Raigad; hill forts and the Maratha navy; the Ashta Pradhan council

t: Starting from his father's jagir at Pune, Shivaji took Bijapuri forts from 1647 and built a state between the Deccan sultanates and the Mughal Empire.
He alternated between war and vassalage with the Mughals, sacking Surat in 1664 and 1670, submitting at Purandar in 1665 and escaping house arrest at Agra in 1666.
Crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674 despite the objection of Brahmins that he was not a Kshatriya, he has since been claimed by reformers, nationalists and Hindutva activists in turn.
dyk: Shivaji replaced Persian with Marathi at his court and had his official Raghunath Pandit compile the Rājavyavahārakośa (1677), a thesaurus replacing Persian and Arabic terms of state with Sanskrit ones.
ev: Shivaji, aged 16, captures Torna Fort and uses its treasure to build Rajgad
He kills the Bijapuri general Afzal Khan at Pratapgad and defeats his army
Shivaji sacks the Mughal port of Surat
By the Treaty of Purandar he gives up 23 forts and becomes a Mughal vassal
Placed under house arrest at Agra, he escapes with his son Sambhaji
Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort
He invades Karnataka and takes Vellore and Gingee

sections.early:
Shivaji was born at the hill-fort of Shivneri near Junnar, in present-day Pune district; scholars disagree on the date, and the Government of Maharashtra marks 19 February as Shivaji Jayanti. He was named after a local goddess, Shivai Devi. His father, Shahaji Bhonsle, was a Maratha general who served the Deccan sultanates, and his mother, Jijabai, was the daughter of Lakhuji Jadhavrao of Sindhkhed, a Mughal-aligned sardar claiming descent from the Yadava kings of Devagiri. His grandfather Maloji had been a general of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate and held deshmukhi rights over Pune and other districts.

Power in the Deccan was then shared between the sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmednagar and Golkonda and the Mughal Empire. Shahaji changed his loyalty often but kept his jagir at Pune and his small army. While the Mughals pursued him, Shivaji and Jijabai moved from fort to fort. In 1636 Shahaji entered Bijapur's service, obtained Poona as a grant and, posted to Bangalore, left Dadoji Kondadeo as its administrator; Shivaji and his mother settled there. The scholar James Laine states that Jijabai, conscious of her Yadava heritage, imbued her son with the dream of re-establishing a Hindu kingdom. When Kondadeo died in 1647, Shivaji took over the administration.
sections.rise:
In 1647, aged 16, Shivaji took Torna Fort by stratagem or bribery during the illness of Sultan Mohammed Adil Shah and used its treasure to build Rajgad, his seat for over a decade. He then took Purandar, Kondhana and Chakan and the town of Kalyan in the Konkan. Bijapur responded by imprisoning his father in 1648, and from 1649 to 1655 Shivaji consolidated quietly. In 1656, under controversial circumstances, he killed the Maratha feudatory Chandrarao More and seized the valley of Javali, and he subdued other Deshmukh families by marriage alliances, dealings with village Patils or force.

In 1657 Bijapur sent the veteran general Afzal Khan against him. On 10 November 1659 the two met in a hut below Pratapgad fort; Shivaji wore armour and hid a bagh nakh, and in a struggle known mainly from Maratha legends he disembowelled Khan. In the Battle of Pratapgarh that followed more than 3,000 Bijapuri soldiers were killed, and the captives were sent home with gifts. Besieged at Panhala by Siddi Jauhar in 1660, Shivaji escaped by night while Baji Prabhu Deshpande and 300 soldiers held the pass later renamed Pavan Khind, and he surrendered the fort on 22 September 1660.
sections.deeds:
Against the Mughals Shivaji raided Junnar in 1657, carrying off 300,000 hun. When Aurangzeb's uncle Shaista Khan occupied Pune, Shivaji with 400 men attacked his mansion on the night of 5 April 1663, wounding him; the general's son and several wives, servants and soldiers were killed. In 1664 he sacked Surat, taking plunder exceeding Rs 10 million. Pressed by Jai Singh I, he signed the Treaty of Purandar on 11 June 1665, giving up 23 forts and becoming a Mughal vassal. Summoned to Agra in 1666 and placed under house arrest, he escaped on 17 August, by the famous story hidden in a basket of sweets; Stewart N. Gordon finds no contemporary evidence for it and thinks he likely bribed the guards.

Peace followed until 1670, when he recovered much of the ceded land, sacked Surat again and defeated a Mughal force at Vani-Dindori. On 6 June 1674 he was crowned at Raigad, taking the titles Chhatrapati and Shakakarta. He then campaigned in the south, made a treaty with Golkonda in 1677 and invaded Karnataka with 30,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry, taking Vellore and Gingee. He ruled through the Ashta Pradhan council of eight ministers, built the Maratha navy with its headquarters at Sindhudurg, and by Jadunath Sarkar's estimate held some 240-280 forts at his death.
sections.opponents:
Shivaji's enemies were Bijapur, the Mughal Empire, the Siddis of Janjira and at times the European companies. He plundered the English factory at Rajapur after its men helped bombard Panhala and never paid the indemnity the English sought. Aurangzeb and his generals called him a "Mountain Rat", and in Mughal eyes he was only a rebel zamindar; Mughal writers called him simply "Shiva", and one recorded his death as "the infidel went to Hell". In 1677 he was defeated by Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar after plundering Srirangapatna. At Purandar he wrote letters to Aurangzeb asking forgiveness and calling himself "the meanest of life-devoting slaves".

His coronation was delayed because Brahmins of his court held that kingship belonged to the Kshatriya varna and that he, of a line of village headmen, was not one. Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi, whom Shivaji is said to have bribed, produced a genealogy of Sisodia descent, which historical evidence suggests is tenuous or invented. Two Brahmins held that his raids had killed Brahmins, cows, women and children, and he paid Rs 8,000 for cleansing. Jadunath Sarkar was criticised for calling the killing of Chandrarao More and his clan a murder. Gijs Kruijtzer argues that the foundations of modern Hindu-Muslim communalism were laid in the interplay between Shivaji and Aurangzeb.
sections.last:
The succession troubled Shivaji's last years. In 1678 he confined his eldest son Sambhaji to Panhala Fort, for an addiction to sensual pleasures or for violating a Brahmin woman; Sambhaji escaped, defected to the Mughals and fought against his father at Bhupalgarh before returning, unrepentant, to confinement. In late March 1680 Shivaji fell ill with fever and dysentery, and he died at Raigad Fort around 3-5 April 1680, aged 50. British records give bloody flux, a Portuguese work anthrax and the Sabhasad Bakhar fever; allegations that his wife Soyarabai poisoned him are doubted by later scholars. His childless eldest surviving wife, Putalabai, committed sati on his funeral pyre.

Soyarabai and several ministers installed her ten-year-old son Rajaram on 21 April 1680. Sambhaji seized Raigad after killing its commander, took control on 18 June and formally ascended the throne on 20 July; Rajaram, his mother and his wife were imprisoned, and Soyarabai was executed for conspiracy in October. The military organisation Shivaji had built, of Maval infantry, Maratha cavalry, forts and a coastal navy, lasted until the end of the Maratha Empire, and Gingee later served as Rajaram's capital.
sections.legacy:
Contemporary English, French, Dutch, Portuguese and Italian writers admired Shivaji's exploits; François Bernier recorded that he spared the Capuchin mission at Surat, and Jadunath Sarkar wrote that his chivalry to women won the admiration even of hostile critics such as Khafi Khan. Many modern commentators deem his religious policy tolerant: he endowed Muslim institutions, had Muslim commanders and a Muslim admiral, Darya Sarang, and urged Aurangzeb to respect Hindu places as Akbar had. Early bakhars present him as an almost divine Hindu king, and scholars hold they must be checked against other sources.

About two centuries after his death Jyotirao Phule portrayed him in 1869 as a hero of the shudras and dalits. From 1895 Bal Gangadhar Tilak held an annual festival for his birthday, and M. G. Ranade's Rise of the Maratha Power (1900) saw in him the beginning of modern nation-building. He is a national hero in India, above all in Maharashtra; the Shiv Sena, formed in 1966, bears his name, and Mumbai's main station, airport and museum were renamed for him. Hindutva activists are noted for presenting him as a Hindu king who fought Muslim rulers, contrary to accounts of his caste and secular values. His depiction stays contested: James W. Laine's 2003 book was banned in Maharashtra in 2004 and the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute attacked, before the courts lifted the ban.

summary: Shivaji built the Maratha Kingdom from his father's jagir at Pune, taking forts from Bijapur, fighting and serving the Mughals in turn, and having himself crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. His guerrilla warfare, forts, navy and Marathi court outlived him, and his memory has been claimed by social reformers, nationalists and Hindutva activists.

notes: Birth date c. 19 February 1630 is disputed (article: scholars disagree). Death 'around 3-5 April 1680'; I set end 1680 not circa.
The article lists the Ashta Pradhan ministers in a table not saved, so I named only the council.
The article's figure of 111 forts built 'according to some accounts' versus 'did not exceed 18' left out for brevity; Sarkar's 240-280 owned kept.
